summary: Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a project that tells the stories of the explorers NASA sent to the Moon and Mars that never returned home. We will discover machines such as the Apollo lunar modules and the Sojourner, Spirit, and Opportunity rovers, learning why they were sent, what adventures they experienced, and what problems caused them to stop working. We will also explore the amazing discoveries they left behind, such as evidence that water once existed on Mars. Because even though these explorers can no longer communicate with us, their tracks and discoveries continue to help us learn more about space.
details: El proyecto "El legado de la NASA que desarrollamos como equipo es una herramienta digital interactiva que creamos en Canva para explorar la historia y el funcionamiento de equipos espaciales inactivos en la Luna y Marte, como los módulos Apolo, los paquetes ALSEP y los rovers Sojourner, Spirit* y Opportunity. En nuestro trabajo, explicamos cómo estos dispositivos fueron diseñados para estudiar el suelo, el clima y los terremotos lunares, destacando también los factores detrás de su eventual silencio, como las tormentas de polvo, las temperaturas bajo cero y la falta de energía. Nuestro principal objetivo y impacto deseado era acercar la ciencia espacial a estudiantes y jóvenes entusiastas de una manera accesible y atractiva, inspirando el interés por las carreras STEM y convirtiendo los datos técnicos en una historia que honrara el legado de estos pioneros de la robótica. Adoptamos un enfoque creativo al enmarcar estas máquinas como "exploradoras con recuerdos" y usar metáforas con las que nos identificamos (como comparar el análisis de rocas con "leer libros del pasado"), adaptando cuidadosamente el tono a nuestro público objetivo, estructurando un viaje claro desde la Luna hasta Marte y creando un diseño visualmente atractivo con imágenes históricas oficiales de la NASA.
dataRefs: The Apollo 11 Lunar Module (LM) "Eagle" was the first crewed vehicle to land on the Moon. It carried two astronauts, Commander Neil A. Armstrong and LM pilot Edwin E. "Buzz" Aldrin, Jr., the first men to walk on the Moon. Also included on the LM was the Early Apollo Scientific Experiment Package (EASEP), which consisted of several self-contained experiments to be deployed and left on the lunar surface, and other scientific and sample collection apparatus.

The LM separated from the Command/Service Module (CSM) at 04:16:03 UT and landed at 06:54:35 UT (1:54:35 a.m. EST) on 19 November 1969 in the Oceanus Procellarum area at 3.0128 S latitude, 23.4219 W longitude (as determined from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images, DE 421 mean Earth/polar rotation axis reference frame) within about 180 meters of the Surveyor 3 spacecraft, which had landed on April 20, 1967. Conrad and Bean took two Moon walks of a total duration of 7 hours 45 minutes covering a total traverse distance of 1.35 km. The first was from 11:32:35 to 15:28:38 UT (6:32 a.m. to 10:28 a.m. EST) and involved sample collections in the vicinity of the LM and deployment of the ALSEP and solar wind composition foil collector. The TV camera was inadvertantly pointed towards the Sun when it was being set up and the vidicon tube was damaged rendering the camera inoperable. On the second of these walks, on November 20 from 03:54:45 to 07:44:00 UT (10:54 p.m. Nov. 19 to 2:44 a.m. Nov. 20 EST) they completed a 1.3 km geology traverse, collecting samples and taking photographs, and visited the Surveyor 3 spacecraft , bringing back about 10 kg of parts for later examination on Earth. They collected a total of 34.35 kg of rock and soil samples and also collected the soalr wind foil. The LM lifted off on 20 November at 14:25:47 UT (9:25 a.m. EST) after spending 31 hours 31 minutes on the Moon. After docking with the CSM (piloted by Richard F. Gordon Jr.) at 17:58:22 UT, the LM was jettisoned at 20:21:30 and intentionally crashed into the Moon, striking at 3.94 S, 338.80 E, about 60 km from the seismic station at the Apollo 12 landing site, creating the first recorded artificial moonquake.
